claims.statement: A precondition failure is a statement about every verdict in the run and still refuses it outright; the per-fault safety net never absorbs one into a single unverifiable claim.

faults.description: The safety net swallows a precondition failure, so a run in which no verdict means anything reports one quiet unverifiable claim and exits on the others.

claims.statement: A probe-error record says something about the run and nothing about the code, so a later run always measures that fault again however unchanged its inputs are.

faults.description: A disturbed run becomes a permanent verdict: the error record is reused for as long as the file is untouched.

claims.statement: A fault that survives is only reported as survived once the defenders are shown to go red when the subject cannot compile; defenders that stay green never execute it, and the verdict is unverifiable instead.

faults.description: The control result is ignored, so a suite that never loads the subject reports every claim about it as SURVIVED — total blindness where there was none.

claims.statement: The negative control asks whether the defenders stayed green, not whether a test failed: a module that cannot parse usually fails to load, which the runner reports as an error with no tests run.

faults.description: Only an assertion failure counts as reached, so every defender that loads the subject is misreported as never executing it and its real verdict is thrown away.

claims.statement: Every runner supplies content for its language that its loader cannot parse; a negative control whose edit still compiles proves nothing.

faults.description: The JavaScript fatal edit parses cleanly, so the control can never turn a suite red and every survivor is rubber-stamped as reached.
faults.find: export const fatalEdit = () => '/* testguard negative control: this file must not parse */\n(\n';
faults.replace: export const fatalEdit = () => '/* testguard negative control */\n';

claims.statement: The negative control replaces the whole subject file and always puts it back; a probe that leaves its own control edit behind has destroyed the thing it was asked to measure.

faults.description: The control never restores, so the subject is left as unparseable rubbish and every later fault is measured against it.

claims.statement: A runner pinned to one engine carries every capability the module has; a capability present on `--runner python` and absent on `--runner pytest` is a silently weaker gate under a flag that reads like a narrowing.

faults.description: The pinned runner drops fatalEdit, so a survivor probed with --runner pytest or --runner unittest is never checked against the negative control and reports survived however unreachable the subject is.
faults.find: return { name: engine, testGlobs, owns, tests, parseReport, fatalEdit, check: makeCheck(engine), run: makeRun(engine) };
faults.replace: return { name: engine, testGlobs, owns, tests, parseReport, check: makeCheck(engine), run: makeRun(engine) };

claims.statement: A probe leaves the tree it was asked to measure byte-identical: every applied fault is restored whatever happens while it is applied, and worktree isolation is never silently replaced by editing the project in place.

faults.description: An applied fault is never restored, so the probe leaves its own edits in the tree and every later fault is measured against corrupted source.
Isolation falls back to editing the project in place, so a probe mutates the source tree it was asked to measure.
faults.find: const iso = mode === 'worktree' ? createScratch({ repoRoot: root, projectDir, ref: snapshot ?? ref, scratchBase, nodeModules }) : inPlace({ repoRoot: root, projectDir });
faults.replace: const iso = inPlace({ repoRoot: root, projectDir });

claims.statement: A document that does not say which method produced it is fault injection, so every claims file, evidence file and baseline written before `method` existed is held to exactly the rules it was written against.

faults.description: An absent method is read as something other than fault injection, so every document written before the field existed silently stops being held to the requirements it was written against.

claims.statement: Relaxing the schema so a scanning tool can conform is never a licence for an injecting tool to stop showing its work: under fault injection every record must still carry its defenders, its inputs and its baseline and probe runs.

faults.description: The injection requirements move out of the schema and are not enforced anywhere, so a verdict with nothing behind it validates.

claims.statement: The escape hatch a reserved method needs is closed to the method that is specified: `methodDetail` is rejected on a fault-injection probe and on an injecting run, so the one shape the spec defines cannot quietly grow undocumented fields.

faults.description: An injecting run may carry methodDetail, so the specified shape acquires a junk drawer nothing validates and no reader can rely on.

claims.statement: The cost budget is a gate, not a number in a log: a probe whose total exceeds the budget fails, and a budget that is missing or not a positive number is refused rather than treated as unlimited.

faults.description: Any total passes the budget, so the check reports success on a gate that has tripled and nothing ever fails.
A missing or malformed budget is accepted instead of refused, so a typo in the budget file silently disables the gate.

claims.statement: A cost-budget failure names the claims that cost the most, by id, from the report as claimCosts actually shapes it; a budget that fails with "undefined" five times has told the reader nothing about where to look.

faults.description: The worst-claims list reads a field the report does not carry, so every name is undefined.

faults.replace: worst: (report.claims ?? []).slice(0, worst).map((c) => ({ id: c.id, ms: c.ms, runs: c.runs })),

claims.statement: Every backoff tier of a calibration is held to the same rules as the primary buckets — arithmetic, ordering, arity. A coarser tier a consumer falls back to is exactly where a wrong number would go unnoticed.

faults.description: Backoff tiers are dropped from the tier list, so only the primary buckets are validated and a wrong interval in a tier passes.

claims.statement: A calibration cell that carries a breakdown of its n by outcome must have that breakdown sum to n; otherwise the narrower rate a consumer recovers from it is wrong.

faults.description: The sum check is removed; any breakdown passes.

claims.statement: The calibration testguard writes says what p measures (escape-missed) and carries the caveat a consumer must show beside any quoted number. Without measures the document is unattributed and nothing may be quoted from it.

faults.description: The emitter stops saying what p measures; the document validates but is unattributed.

claims.statement: A proposed fault always changes the line it anchors to. A replacement equal to its find is rejected by the schema, so a single one aborts the whole scaffold run — one `expired: 0` made a 725-line file impossible to scaffold. Each numeric producer refuses its own fixed point where it knows the arithmetic, and a zero-valued window is still widened to a real value rather than dropped: 0 is exactly the window worth widening.

faults.description: A zero-valued window widens to itself: ×1000 of 0 is 0, the replacement equals the find, and the run aborts.
A work factor already at 1 is collapsed to 1: the same no-op, from the other numeric producer.
faults.find: if (Number(m[3]) > 1) out.push({ faultClass: 'literal-changed', description: `Work factor collapsed: \`${m[1]}\` ${m[3]} becomes 1.`, replace: line.replace(m[0], `${m[1]}${m[2] === ':' ? ': ' : ' = '}1`) });
faults.replace: out.push({ faultClass: 'literal-changed', description: `Work factor collapsed: \`${m[1]}\` ${m[3]} becomes 1.`, replace: line.replace(m[0], `${m[1]}${m[2] === ':' ? ': ' : ' = '}1`) });

faults.description: The backstop stops refusing a no-op, so a producer added later can abort a whole scaffold run again.
Python: a zero-valued window widens to itself. `timeout=0` is PEP 8 spacing, so this is the common form.

claims.statement: `if (…) continue;` and `if (…) break;` are guards and are proposed as faults. Pure selection-over-rows is the shape the “pure logic, caller does the IO” advice produces, and scaffold returned nothing at all for two fully-claimed files of seven such guards each — while the hand-written faults on those same lines all killed. The shape scaffold skipped was the one demonstrably worth proposing.

faults.description: A block guard whose body only continues or breaks is no longer read as a guard.
A single-line `if (…) continue;` no longer matches the if-shape at all, so nothing is proposed for it.
Python: a loop guard is no longer read as a guard.

claims.statement: `p` is computed over escaped BUGS, not over every commit that changed source and a test together. Where a repository labels its commits a `feat:` is not a bug: a run measured “12 of 12 measurable bugs invisible — 100%” over a corpus of five features, a refactor, a style change and a commit whose whole purpose was adding a test. Selection stays broad, the estimator narrows, and the document records which rule produced it so two calibrations can never be compared by accident.

faults.description: The corpus stops narrowing: features and chores are counted as escaped bugs again.
The calibration stops recording which rule produced it, so two different populations carry the same shape.

claims.statement: An unexpected exception reaches the user as a testguard bug with its trace, never as a bare Node stack. A producer defect printed `Node.js v24.18.0` at someone debugging their own project; a tool whose thesis is “never optimistic, always legible” owes the operator the sentence that says whose fault it is. The trace stays: a framed error without one cannot be reported.

faults.description: The unexpected error is re-thrown, so the user gets a raw Node stack trace instead of a named finding.
faults.find: io.err(`error: this is a bug in testguard ${VERSION}, not a problem with your project.`);

claims.statement: A runner that exited between the process snapshot and the warning is not reported as contention. `ps` is a snapshot; a suite that finishes in that window produced “1 test runner is already running (pid 65751)” for a process the operator could not find. Detection stays best-effort — it may under-report — but it may not invent load that is not there.

faults.description: The liveness re-check is dropped, so a pid that has already exited is warned about.

claims.statement: The regenerated `.testguard/` outputs are named in exactly one place. `baseline` kept its own copy and printed two filenames long after the tool wrote ten, and printed them every run whether or not the project was already covered. One list, owned by `init`, read by both.

faults.description: The outputs that shipped after the advice was written fall off the list again, so a project is told to ignore a set that no longer matches what the tool writes.

claims.statement: A claim over the per-claim ceiling fails the gate even when the total is comfortably inside its budget. The total alone cannot see this: a calibration claim cost 51 s for two faults purely by naming replay.test.mjs instead of calibration.test.mjs, and re-pointing it took it to 4.9 s while the total never moved. A per-fault average cannot see it either - the regression that prompted this budget raised the fault count 59 to 91 while per-fault cost barely moved. The ceiling is optional and additive: a budget without one behaves exactly as it did.

faults.description: A claim over the ceiling no longer fails the gate: the per-claim result is computed and then ignored in the verdict.
The ceiling stops being applied at all, so every claim passes however expensive it is.
A breach stops naming the claims it found, so the operator is told a number is wrong but not which claim to look at.
faults.find: for (const c of d.overPerClaim) out.push(`  ${secs(c.ms).padStart(7)}  ${c.id}  (${c.runs} runs)`);

claims.statement: The technical brief's PDF is rendered from its HTML and can never silently disagree with it: the release runs build-one-pager.mjs with --require-chrome, so a machine without a browser fails the release instead of leaving the committed PDF stale at exit 0, and every render is rejected unless it produced exactly one sheet per `.page` div — a section that overflows its sheet spills onto a second one with no warning from Chrome, contradicting the "Page N of M" footers the document prints about itself.

faults.description: A render that spilled onto extra sheets is accepted; the brief ships with pages its own footers do not number.
--require-chrome stops requiring Chrome; a release on a runner without one skips the render at exit 0 and commits a PDF whose masthead names the previous version.

claims.statement: Every exact fault anchor and every supported replacement is validated before the long self-probe starts. A missing or ambiguous anchor, or a JavaScript/Python replacement that does not parse, exits 1 with the claim, fault, file and hit counts; status points at the fault definition to repair, and CI cannot continue to self-probe past a failed preflight.

faults.description: Invalid anchors are counted as valid, so the command exits 0 over a fault it could not apply.
Status ignores invalid anchors and falls through to an evidence state instead of directing repair.
CI replaces the anchor preflight with a harmless command, so a rotted fault spends the self-probe budget before failing.

claims.statement: Every GITHUB_TOKEN-authored release pull request clears first-time-contributor workflow holds before its creating workflow succeeds. Both the scheduled version PR and the post-publish Homebrew checksum PR use one fail-closed helper, so an API failure or a hold that remains visible is an error rather than a silently queued auto-merge.

faults.description: The post-publish Homebrew PR skips the approval helper and can remain queued after the release workflow reports success.
The scheduled release PR stops using the shared approval helper, allowing the two bot-created PR paths to drift again.
A failed GitHub API query is treated as an empty hold list, so the helper reports success without knowing whether auto-merge is blocked.

claims.statement: The root Vitest gate describes only this checkout: it never collects fixtures or agent-managed nested worktrees under .claude, so parked unmerged work cannot create false failures in npm test.

faults.description: The root test boundary stops excluding agent-managed nested worktrees, so npm test can collect an unrelated checkout.

claims.statement: Status reports how many current source modules carry a claim, names concrete unclaimed modules ranked by bounded recent churn without collapsing churn and path risk into a score, and directs a clean project to expand the denominator while most modules remain unclaimed.

faults.description: Test files replace source modules in the denominator, so claimed surface no longer describes production code.
Unclaimed modules are ranked from least changed to most changed, pointing the next action away from the highest-churn gap.
A clean project expands its denominator only when fewer modules are unclaimed than claimed, preserving the misleading early-adoption green.

claims.statement: The human-facing probe summary and status rendering both warn when killed faults were caught by tests co-authored with the code they defend; the evidence-quality caveat is never confined to JSON or the agent brief.

faults.description: Probe computes the co-authored count but drops the warning from its human summary.
Status drops the co-authorship warning while retaining the count in its JSON document.

claims.statement: Every repeated or comma-separated probe --claim value is retained in first-seen order, duplicates are collapsed, and partial output reports requested versus probed scope instead of silently presenting a smaller green run.

faults.description: The global parser returns to last-wins semantics, silently dropping every repeated claim selection before probe can see it.
Normalized claim ids are sorted instead of retaining first-seen order.
Partial scope claims everything requested was probed, hiding an incomplete run.
The engine restores claims-file order instead of the operator's requested order.
Scaffold silently accepts repeated singular claim values.
Admit silently accepts repeated singular claim values.
The published status schema stops accepting probe run metadata, returning probe JSON to an undocumented wrapper.
The semantic validator stops checking requested counts against the ids they summarize.
